n:
*Translator's note:* *Grk* “It happened that when.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated. Since the action described by the participle ἀποσπασθέντας (apospasthentas, “tearing ourselves away”) is prior to the departure of the ship, it has been translated as antecedent action (“after”).

*Study note:* This marks the beginning of one of the “*we*” sections in Acts ({{Acts 16:10|16:10-17}}; {{Acts 20:5|20:5-15}}; {{Acts 21:1|21:1-18}}; {{Acts 27:1|27:1-28:16}}). These have been traditionally understood to mean that the author was in the company of Paul for this part of the journey.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 120 s.v. ἀποσπάω 2.b has “pass. in mid. sense ἀ. ἀπό τινος *tear oneself away* {{Acts 21:1|Ac 21:1}}”; LSJ 218 gives several illustrations of this verb meaning “*to tear* or *drag away* from.”

*Translator's note:* BDAG 62 s.v. ἀνάγω 4, “as a nautical t.t. (ἀ. τὴν ναῦν put a ship to sea), mid. or pass. ἀνάγεσθαι to begin to go by boat, *put out to sea*.”

*Translator's note:* BDAG 406 s.v. εὐθυδρομέω has “of a ship *run a straight course*”; L&N 54.3 has “to sail a straight course, sail straight to.”

*Study note:* *Cos* was an island in the Aegean Sea.

*Study note:* *Rhodes* was an island off the southwestern coast of Asia Minor.

*Study note:* *Patara* was a city in Lycia on the southwestern coast of Asia Minor. The entire journey was about 185 mi (295 km).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and finding.” The participle εὑρόντες (heurontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. Because of the length of the Greek sentence, the conjunction καί (kai) has not been translated here. Instead a new English sentence is begun in the translation.

*Study note:* *Phoenicia* was the name of an area along the Mediterranean coast north of Palestine.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “going aboard, we put out to sea.” The participle ἐπιβάντες (epibantes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 62 s.v. ἀνάγω 4, “as a nautical t.t. (ἀ. τὴν ναῦν put a ship to sea), mid. or pass. ἀνάγεσθαι to begin to go by boat, *put out to sea*.”

*Study note:* *Cyprus* is a large island in the Mediterranean off the south coast of Asia Minor.

*Study note:* The expression *left it behind on our port side* here means “sailed past to the south of it” since the ship was sailing east.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 531 s.v. κατέρχομαι 2 states, “*arrive, put in,* nautical t.t. of ships and those who sail in them, who ‘come down’ fr. the ‘high seas’…ἔις τι *at someth*. a harbor {{Acts 18:22|18:22}}; {{Acts 21:3|21:3}}; {{Acts 27:5|27:5}}.”

*Study note:* *Tyre* was a city and seaport on the coast of Phoenicia. From Patara to Tyre was about 400 mi (640 km). It required a large cargo ship over 100 ft (30 m) long, and was a four to five day voyage.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 78 s.v. ἀνευρίσκω has “*look/search for* (w. finding presupposed) τινά…τοὺς μαθητάς {{Acts 21:4|Ac 21:4}}.” The English verb “locate,” when used in reference to persons, has the implication of both looking for and finding someone. The participle ἀνευρόντες (aneurontes) has been taken temporally.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 154 s.v. αὐτοῦ states, “deictic adv. designating a position relatively near or far…*there*…{{Acts 21:4|Ac 21:4}}.”

*Translator's note:* The imperfect verb ἔλεγον (elegon) has been taken iteratively.

*Study note:* Although they told this to Paul *through the Spirit*, it appears Paul had a choice here (see v. {{Acts 21:14|14}}). Therefore this amounted to a warning: There was risk in going to Jerusalem, so he was urged not to go.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 367 s.v. ἐπιβαίνω places {{Acts 21:4|Ac 21:4}} under 1, “*go up/upon, mount, board*…πλοίῳ…{{Acts 27:2|Ac 27:2}}…Abs. *go on board, embark*…{{Acts 21:1|21:1}} D, 2.—So perh. also ἐ. εἰς ᾿Ιεροσόλυμα *embark for Jerusalem* (i.e., to the seaport of Caesarea) vs. {{Acts 21:4|4}}.” BDAG notes, however, “But this pass. may also belong to 2. to move to an area and be there, *set foot in*.” Because the message from the disciples to Paul through the Holy Spirit has the character of a warning, the latter meaning has been adopted for this translation.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “It happened that when.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “When our days were over.” L&N 67.71 has “ὅτε δὲ ἐγένετο ἡμᾶς ἐξαρτίσαι τὰς ἡμέρας ‘when we brought that time to an end’ or ‘when our time with them was over’ {{Acts 21:5|Ac 21:5}}.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “accompanying.” Due to the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was begun in the translation and the participle προπεμπόντων (propempontōn) translated as a finite verb.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “city, and after.” Because of the length of the Greek sentence, the conjunction καί (kai) has not been translated here. Instead a new English sentence is begun.

*Study note:* On *praying* in Acts, see {{Acts 1:14|1:14}}, {{Acts 1:24|24}}; {{Acts 2:47|2:47}}; {{Acts 4:23|4:23}}; {{Acts 6:6|6:6}}; {{Acts 10:2|10:2}}; {{Acts 12:5|12:5}}, {{Acts 12:12|12}}; {{Acts 13:3|13:3}}; {{Acts 16:25|16:25}}.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 98 s.v. ἀπασπάζομαι has “*take leave of, say farewell to* τινά *someone*…ἀπησπασάμεθα ἀλλήλους *we said farewell to one another* {{Acts 21:6|Ac 21:6}}.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was begun in the translation, and καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the logical sequence.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “to their own”; the word “homes” is implied.

*Study note:* *Tyre* was a city and seaport on the coast of Phoenicia.

*Study note:* *Ptolemais* was a seaport on the coast of Palestine about 30 mi (48 km) south of Tyre.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “On the next day leaving, we came.” The participle ἐξελθόντες (exelthontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

*Study note:* *Caesarea* was a city on the coast of Palestine south of Mount Carmel (not Caesarea Philippi). See the note on *Caesarea* in {{Acts 10:1|Acts 10:1}}. This was another 40 mi (65 km).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and entering…we stayed.” The participle εἰσελθόντες (eiselthontes) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

*Study note:* Philip was *one of the seven* deacons appointed in the Jerusalem church ({{Acts 6:1|Acts 6:1-7}}).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “virgin.” While the term παρθένος (parthenos) can refer to a woman who has never had sexual relations, the emphasis in this context seems to be on the fact that Philip’s daughters were not married (L&N 9.39).

*Study note:* This is best taken as a parenthetical note by the author. Luke again noted women who were gifted in the early church (see Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 3.31; 3.39).

*Translator's note:* BDAG 848 s.v. πολύς 1.b.α has “ἐπὶ ἡμέρας πλείους *for a (large) number of days, for many days*…{{Acts 13:31|Ac 13:31}}.—{{Acts 21:10|21:10}}…{{Acts 24:17|24:17}}; {{Acts 25:14|25:14}}; {{Acts 27:20|27:20}}.”

*Study note:* *Agabus* also appeared in {{Acts 11:28|Acts 11:28}}. He was from Jerusalem, so the two churches were still in contact with one another.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “And coming.” Because of the difference between Greek style, which often begins sentences or clauses with “and,” and English style, which generally does not, καί (kai) has not been translated here. The participle ἐλθών (elthōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and taking.” This καί (kai) has not been translated since English normally uses a coordinating conjunction only between the last two elements in a series of three or more. The participle ἄρας (aras) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

*Study note:* The *belt* was a band or sash used to keep money as well as to gird up the tunic (BDAG 431 s.v. ζώνη).

*Translator's note:* The participle δήσας (dēsas) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

*Translator's note:* The words “with it” are not in the Greek text, but are implied.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and will deliver him over into the hands of” (a Semitic idiom).

*Study note:* *The Jews…will tie up…and will hand him over*. As later events will show, the Jews in Jerusalem did not personally tie Paul up and hand him over to the Gentiles, but their reaction to him was the cause of his arrest ({{Acts 21:27|Acts 21:27-36}}).

*Translator's note:* The term translated “breaking” as used by Josephus (*Ant*. 10.10.4 [10.207]) means to break something into pieces, but in its only NT use (it is a *hapax legomenon*) it is used figuratively (BDAG 972 s.v. συνθρύπτω).

*Translator's note:* L&N 18.13 has “to tie objects together—‘to tie, to tie together, to tie up.’” The verb δέω (deō) is sometimes figurative for imprisonment (L&N 37.114), but it is preferable to translate it literally here in light of v. {{Acts 21:11|11}} where Agabus tied himself up with Paul’s belt.

*Translator's note:* The participle πειθομένου (peithomenou) in this genitive absolute construction has been translated as a causal adverbial participle.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “we became silent, saying.”

*Study note:* *“The Lord’s will be done.”* Since no one knew exactly what would happen, the matter was left in the Lord’s hands.

*Translator's note:* Or “we made preparations.”

*Study note:* In colloquial speech Jerusalem was always said to be “*up*” from any other location in Palestine. The group probably covered the 65 mi (105 km) in two days using horses. Their arrival in Jerusalem marked the end of Paul’s third missionary journey.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “were going up”; the imperfect verb ἀνεβαίνομεν (anebainomen) has been translated as an ingressive imperfect.

*Study note:* *Caesarea* was a city on the coast of Palestine south of Mount Carmel (not Caesarea Philippi). See the note on *Caesarea* in {{Acts 10:1|Acts 10:1}}.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “to Mnason…”; the words “the house of” are not in the Greek text, but are implied by the verb ξενισθῶμεν (xenisthōmen).

*Translator's note:* Or perhaps, “Mnason of Cyprus, one of the original disciples.” BDAG 137 s.v. ἀρχαῖος 1 has “ἀ. μαθητής *a disciple of long standing* (perh. *original disc*.) {{Acts 21:16|Ac 21:16}}.”

*Study note:* *All the elders were there*. This meeting shows how the Jerusalem church still regarded Paul and his mission with favor, but also with some concerns because of the rumors circulating about his actions.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 760 s.v. παραγίνομαι 1 has this use under the broad category of meaning “*draw near, come, arrive, be present*.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “he”; the referent (Paul) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* Or “to report,” “to describe.” The imperfect verb ἐξηγεῖτο (exēgeito) has been translated as an ingressive imperfect.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 293 s.v. εἷς 5.e has “καθ᾿ ἕν *one after the other* (hence τὸ καθ᾿ ἕν ‘a detailed list’: PLille 11, 8 [III bc]; PTebt. 47, 34; 332, 16) J 21:25. Also καθ᾿ ἕν ἕκαστον…{{Acts 21:19|Ac 21:19}}.”

*Study note:* Note how Paul credited *God* with the success of his ministry.

*Translator's note:* Or “glorified.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “how many thousands there are among the Jews.”

*Study note:* *How many thousands of Jews*. See {{Acts 2|Acts 2-5}} for the accounts of their conversion, esp. {{Acts 2:41|2:41}} and {{Acts 4:4|4:4}}. Estimates of the total number of Jews living in Jerusalem at the time range from 20,000 to 50,000.

*Translator's note:* Or “are all zealous for the law.” BDAG 427 s.v. ζηλωτής 1.a.β has “of thing…τοῦ νόμου *an ardent observer of the law* {{Acts 21:20|Ac 21:20}}.”

*Study note:* That is, the *law* of Moses. These Jewish Christians had remained close to their Jewish practices after becoming believers (1 Cor 7:18-19; {{Acts 16:3|Acts 16:3}}).

*Translator's note:* BDAG 511 s.v. κατά B.1.a has “τοὺς κ. τὰ ἔθνη ᾿Ιουδαίους *the Judeans (dispersed) throughout the nations* 21:21.” The Jews in view are not those in Palestine, but those who are scattered throughout the Gentile world.

*Study note:* The charge that Paul was teaching Jews in the Diaspora *to abandon Moses* was different from the issue faced in {{Acts 15|Acts 15}}, where the question was whether Gentiles needed to become like Jews first in order to become Christians. The issue also appears in {{Acts 24:5|Acts 24:5-6}}, {{Acts 24:13|13-21}}; {{Acts 25:8|25:8}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “to forsake,” “to rebel against.” BDAG 120 s.v. ἀποστασία has “ἀποστασίαν διδάσκεις ἀπὸ Μωϋσέως *you teach (Judeans) to abandon Moses* {{Acts 21:21|Ac 21:21}}.”

*Study note:* That is, not to circumcise their male children. Biblical references to circumcision always refer to male circumcision.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “or walk.”
*Translator's note:* L&N 71.16 has “pertaining to being in every respect certain—‘certainly, really, doubtless, no doubt.’…‘they will no doubt hear that you have come’ {{Acts 21:22|Ac 21:22}}.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “do this that.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “There are four men here.”

*Translator's note:* L&N 33.469 has “‘there are four men here who have taken a vow’ or ‘we have four men who…’ {{Acts 21:23|Ac 21:23}}.”

*Translator's note:* On the term for “vow,” see BDAG 416 s.v. εὐχή 2.

*Study note:* That is, undergo ritual cleansing. Paul’s cleansing would be necessary because of his travels in “unclean” Gentile territory. This act would represent a conciliatory gesture. Paul would have supported a “law-free” mission to the Gentiles as an option, but this gesture would represent an attempt to be sensitive to the Jews (1 Cor 9:15-22).

*Translator's note:* L&N 57.146 has “δαπάνησον ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς ‘pay their expenses’ {{Acts 21:24|Ac 21:24}}.”

*Study note:* Having *their heads shaved* probably involved ending a voluntary Nazirite vow ({{Numbers 6:14|Num 6:14-15}}).

*Translator's note:* The future middle indicative has causative force here. BDAG 686 s.v. ξυράω has “mid. *have oneself shaved*…τὴν κεφαλήν *have one*’*s head shaved*…{{Acts 21:24|Ac 21:24}}.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was begun in the translation, and καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the logical sequence.

*Translator's note:* The verb here describes a report or some type of information (BDAG 534 s.v. κατηχέω 1).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “adhere to the keeping of the law.” L&N 41.12 has “στοιχέω: to live in conformity with some presumed standard or set of customs—‘to live, to behave in accordance with.’”

*Study note:* *The law* refers to the law of Moses.

*Study note:* *Having decided* refers here to the decision of the Jerusalem council ({{Acts 15:6|Acts 15:6-21}}). Mention of this previous decision reminds the reader that the issue here is somewhat different: It is not whether Gentiles must first become Jews before they can become Christians (as in {{Acts 15|Acts 15}}), but whether Jews who become Christians should retain their Jewish practices. Sensitivity to this issue would suggest that Jewish Christians and Gentile Christians might engage in different practices.

*Translator's note:* L&N 13.154 has “‘having decided that they must keep themselves from food offered to idols, from blood, from an animal that has been strangled, and from sexual immorality’ {{Acts 21:25|Ac 21:25}}.”

*Translator's note:* This is a different Greek word than the one used in {{Acts 15:20|Acts 15:20}}, {{Acts 15:29|29}}. BDAG 1068 s.v. φυλάσσω 3 has “to be on one’s guard against*, look out for,* avoid…w. acc. of pers. or thing avoided…{{Acts 21:25|Ac 21:25}}.” The Greek word used in {{Acts 15:20|Acts 15:20}}, {{Acts 15:29|29}} is ἀπέχω (apechō). The difference in meaning, although slight, has been maintained in the translation.

*Translator's note:* There is no specific semantic component in the Greek word εἰδωλόθυτος that means “meat” (see BDAG 280 s.v. εἰδωλόθυτος; L&N 5.15). The stem—θυτος means “sacrifice” (referring to an animal sacrificially killed) and thereby implies meat.

*Study note:* *What has been strangled*. That is, to refrain from eating animals that had been killed without having the blood drained from them. According to the Mosaic law (Lev 17:13-14) Jews were forbidden to eat flesh with the blood still in it (note the preceding provision in this verse, *and blood*).

*Translator's note:* BDAG 422 s.v. ἔχω 11.b.β has “temporal, to be next, *immediately following*…τῇ ἐχομένῃ…*on the next day* Lk 13:33…{{Acts 20:15|Ac 20:15}}; w. ἡμέρᾳ added…21:26.”

*Translator's note:* That is, after he had undergone ritual cleansing. The aorist passive participle ἁγνισθείς (hagnistheis) has been taken temporally of antecedent action.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “entered the temple, giving notice.” The participle διαγγέλλων (diangellōn) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

*Study note:* The *days of purification* refers to the days of ritual cleansing.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “until” (BDAG 423 s.v. ἕως 1.b.β.א), but since in English it is somewhat awkward to say “the completion of the days of purification, until the sacrifice would be offered,” the temporal clause was translated “when the sacrifice would be offered.” The point is that the sacrifice would be offered when the days were completed. Paul honored the request of the Jewish Christian leadership completely. As the following verse makes clear, the vow was made for seven days.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “for each one.”

*Translator's note:* BDAG 975 s.v. συντελέω 4 has “to come to an end of a duration, *come to an end, be over*…{{Acts 21:27|Ac 21:27}}.”

*Study note:* Note how there is a sense of Paul being pursued from a distance. These Jews may well have been from Ephesus, since they recognized Trophimus the Ephesian (v. {{Acts 21:29|29}}).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “Asia”; in the NT this always refers to the Roman province of Asia. The Roman province of Asia made up about one-third of modern Asia Minor and was on the western side of it. Asia lay to the west of the region of Phrygia and Galatia. The words “the province of” are supplied to indicate to the modern reader that this does not refer to the continent of Asia.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “in the temple.” See the note on the word “temple” in v. {{Acts 21:28|28}}.

*Translator's note:* Or “threw the whole crowd into consternation.” L&N 25.221 has “συνέχεον πάντα τὸν ὄχλον ‘they threw the whole crowd into consternation’ {{Acts 21:27|Ac 21:27}}. It is also possible to render the expression in {{Acts 21:27|Ac 21:27}} as ‘they stirred up the whole crowd.’”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and laid hands on.”

*Translator's note:* Or “Israelite men,” although this is less natural English. The Greek term here is ἀνήρ (anēr), which only exceptionally is used in a generic sense of both males and females. In this context, it is conceivable that this is a generic usage since “the whole crowd” is mentioned in v. {{Acts 21:27|27}}, although it can also be argued that these remarks were addressed primarily to the men present, even if women were there.

*Study note:* *The law* refers to the law of Moses.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “this place.”

*Study note:* *This sanctuary* refers to the temple. The charges were not new, but were similar to those made against Stephen ({{Acts 6:14|Acts 6:14}}) and Jesus (Luke 23:2).

*Translator's note:* BDAG 400 s.v. ἔτι 2.b has “ἔ. δὲ καί *furthermore*…al. ἔ. τε καί…Lk 14:26; {{Acts 21:28|Ac 21:28}}.” This is a continuation of the same sentence in Greek, but due to the length and complexity of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English to use shorter sentences, a new sentence was begun here in the translation.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “into the temple.” The specific reference is to the Court of the Sons of Israel (see the note following the term “unclean” at the end of this verse). To avoid giving the modern reader the impression that they entered the temple building itself, the phrase “the inner courts of the temple” has been used in the translation.

*Study note:* *Has brought Greeks…unclean*. Note how the issue is both religious and ethnic, showing a different attitude by the Jews. A Gentile was not permitted to enter the inner temple precincts (contrast {{Ephesians 2:11|Eph 2:11-22}}). According to Josephus (*Ant*. 15.11.5 [15.417]; *J. W*. 5.5.2 [5.193], cf. 5.5.6 [5.227]), the inner temple courts (the Court of the Women, the Court of the Sons of Israel, and the Court of the Priests) were raised slightly above the level of the Court of the Gentiles and were surrounded by a wall about 5 ft (1.5 m) high. Notices in both Greek and Latin (two of which have been discovered) warned that any Gentiles who ventured into the inner courts would be responsible for their own deaths. See also Philo, *Embassy* 31 (212). In *m. Middot* 2:3 this wall was called “*soreq*” and according to *m. Sanhedrin* 9:6 the stranger who trespassed beyond the *soreq* would die by the hand of God.

*Translator's note:* Or “and has defiled this holy place.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “whom.”

*Translator's note:* On the phrase “inner temple courts” see the note on the word “temple” in v. {{Acts 21:28|28}}.

*Study note:* This is a parenthetical note by the author. The note explains the cause of the charge and also notes that it was false.

*Translator's note:* On this term see BDAG 545 s.v. κινέω 2.b.

*Translator's note:* Or “the people formed a mob.” BDAG 967 s.v. συνδρομή has “formation of a mob by pers. running together, *running together*…ἐγένετο σ. τοῦ λαοῦ *the people rushed together* {{Acts 21:30|Ac 21:30}}.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and seizing.” The participle ἐπιλαβόμενοι (epilabomenoi) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style. Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was begun in the translation, and καί (kai) has not been translated here.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “out of the temple.” See the note on the word “temple” in v. {{Acts 21:28|28}}.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “seeking.”

*Translator's note:* Or “information” (originally concerning a crime; BDAG 1050 s.v. φάσις).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “went up”; this verb is used because the report went up to the Antonia Fortress where the Roman garrison was stationed.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “the chiliarch” (an officer in command of a thousand soldiers). In Greek the term χιλίαρχος (chiliarchos) literally described the “commander of a thousand,” but it was used as the standard translation for the Latin *tribunus militum* or *tribunus militare*, the military tribune who commanded a cohort of 600 men.

*Study note:* A *cohort* was a Roman military unit of about 600 soldiers, one-tenth of a legion.

*Translator's note:* BDAG 953 s.v. συγχέω has “Pass. w. act.force *be in confusion*…ὅλη συγχύννεται ᾿Ιερουσαλήμ 21:31.”

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “who.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence and the tendency of contemporary English to use shorter sentences, the relative pronoun (“who”) was translated as a pronoun (“he”) and a new sentence was begun here in the translation.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “taking…ran down.” The participle κατέδραμεν (katedramen) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

*Study note:* See the note on the word *centurion* in {{Acts 10:1|10:1}}.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “to them”; the referent (the crowd) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “seeing.” The participle ἰδόντες (idontes) has been taken temporally.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “the chiliarch” (an officer in command of a thousand soldiers). See note on the term “commanding officer” in v. {{Acts 21:31|31}}.

*Study note:* The mob *stopped beating Paul* because they feared the Romans would arrest them for disturbing the peace and for mob violence. They would let the Roman officials take care of the matter from this point on.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “the chiliarch” (an officer in command of a thousand soldiers). See note on the term “commanding officer” in v. {{Acts 21:31|31}}.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “seized.”

*Translator's note:* The *two chains* would be something like handcuffs (BDAG 48 s.v. ἅλυσις and compare {{Acts 28:20|Acts 28:20}}).

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and he.” Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was begun in the translation, and καί (kai) has been replaced with a semicolon. “Then” has been supplied after “he” to clarify the logical sequence.

*Translator's note:* *Grk* “and what it is”; this has been simplified to “what.”

*Translator's note:* L&N 33.77 has “ἄλλοι δὲ ἄλλο τι ἐπεφώνουν ἐν τῷ ὄχλῳ ‘some in the crowd shouted one thing; others, something else’ {{Acts 21:34|Ac 21:34}}.”

*Study note:* *That had the* ‘*Heavenly Twins*’ *as its figurehead*. The twin brothers Castor and Pollux, known collectively as the *Dioscuri* or ‘Heavenly Twins,’ were the twin sons of Zeus and Leda according to Greek mythology. The Alexandrian ship on which Paul and his companions sailed from Malta had a carved emblem or figurehead of these figures, and they would have been the patron deities of the vessel. Castor and Pollux were the “gods of navigation.” To see their stars was considered a good omen (Epictetus, *Discourses* 2.18.29; Lucian of Samosata, *The Ship* 9).

*Study note:* *Testifying about the kingdom of God*. The topic is important. Paul’s preaching was about the rule of God and his promise in Jesus. Paul’s text was the Jewish scriptures. This is yet another summary of the message like that in {{Acts 18:28|18:28}}. The nature of the kingdom of God in the NT and in Jesus’ teaching (along with Paul’s teaching here) has long been debated by interpreters and scholars, with discussion primarily centering around the nature of the kingdom (earthly, heavenly, or both) and the kingdom’s arrival (present, future, or both). An additional major issue concerns the relationship between the kingdom of God and the person and work of Jesus himself. See also Luke 6:20; 11:20; 17:20-21; {{Acts 1:3|Acts 1:3}}.
